passage:
Omkar,
I owe you an apology, a proper one, not a quick "sorry" in the corridor.
When the class trip money went missing from the monitor's desk, I told Ma'am I was sure it was you. You wouldn't look at anyone, you kept tapping your pen, and your voice went shaky. I thought that was proof.
Yesterday the money turned up in the sports-room register, where the monitor had left it. Nobody took it.
My cousin, who studies psychology, told me that nervous people telling the truth can look exactly like that, and people who lie can look perfectly calm. I didn't know that. You were probably nervous because I was staring at you.
I'm sorry I made the whole class look at you that way. I'll tell Ma'am too.
Kiran

qa.q: Where did the trip money turn up?
qa.a: In the sports-room register, where the monitor had left it.

qa.q: Why was Kiran so sure Omkar had taken the money?
qa.a: Kiran believed that not looking at anyone, tapping a pen and a shaky voice were proof of lying.

qa.q: What could Kiran do differently the next time something goes missing?
qa.a: Kiran could check the facts first, such as where the money was last kept, instead of reading guilt from nervousness.

qa.q: What was it like for Omkar to be suspected in front of the class?
qa.a: Omkar was probably frightened and humiliated, and being stared at likely made the nervousness even stronger.

grounding: A teenager who took fidgeting and avoided eye contact as proof of lying learns such cues are weak, since nervous truth-tellers look the same.

passage:
What did I learn in Class 11? That I'm terrible at spotting liars. I'm Baljeet, and so is everyone, probably.
During the student council election, someone ran an anonymous page mocking the candidates. Everyone suspected a quiet boy from 11C, because when the teacher questioned him he stammered, went red and stared at his shoes. I was sure too.
Then my friend Bidisha looked me straight in the eye and said, "It's horrible. I'd never do that." Totally calm. I believed her completely.
Two weeks later the school found the page had been made from her account.
So now when someone says "you can tell by their eyes", I think of that boy's red face and Bidisha's steady one. I check facts now, not faces.

qa.q: What did Bidisha say when asked about the page?
qa.a: "It's horrible. I'd never do that."

qa.q: Why did Baljeet believe Bidisha so completely?
qa.a: Bidisha looked Baljeet straight in the eye and stayed totally calm, which Baljeet took as a sign of honesty.

qa.q: What does Baljeet do now instead of reading faces?
qa.a: Baljeet checks facts, not faces, since both the steady eyes and the red cheeks turned out to be misleading.

qa.q: How might the quiet boy from 11C have felt while everyone suspected him?
qa.a: He likely felt scared and ashamed, which made him stammer and go red even though he had done nothing.

grounding: A teenager learns that a calm, eye-contact denial and a stammering, red-faced one say little about who is honest.

passage:
I'm Vandana, and I sit two benches behind Lokesh in Class 10. When Priyanka's new calculator went missing after the maths period, I was sure it was him.
Ma'am asked everyone, "Did anyone take it?" Lokesh went red, looked at the floor and kept pulling at his collar. He couldn't even meet her eyes. Liar, I thought. Obviously.
Meanwhile Jatin, sitting beside him, looked straight at Ma'am and said calmly, "No, Ma'am. I didn't see it."
At the end of the day, the calculator fell out of Jatin's bag when he pulled out his water bottle.
I sat there feeling stupid. Lokesh, it turned out, goes red whenever a teacher looks at him, about anything. Later I heard him say to a friend, "I always look guilty. I hate it."
I had been so sure. I had been completely wrong.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do when Ma'am asked the class?
qa.a: Lokesh went red, looked at the floor and kept pulling at his collar.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel when the calculator fell out of Jatin's bag?
qa.a: Vandana felt stupid and ashamed, realising the nervous signs had fooled her completely.

qa.q: What could Vandana do next time she suspects someone?
qa.a: She could wait for real evidence instead of reading nervousness as guilt, and remember that calm faces can hide lies too.

qa.q: How does Lokesh feel about the way he reacts?
qa.a: Lokesh feels frustrated and embarrassed, hating that he always looks guilty even when he is innocent.

grounding: A classmate observes that nervous signs like avoiding eye contact were wrongly read as lying, while the calm student was the one who took it.

passage:
Sunday. Pooja found her headphones on the floor of her room, one earpiece snapped off. Her little brother Chetan was in the doorway. When she asked, he looked at the ceiling and fidgeted with his shirt. "I didn't touch them." Pooja was sure he was lying. Who else fidgets like that?
Tuesday. She didn't talk to him at breakfast. She told Mummy he was a liar. Chetan's eyes filled with tears. "I didn't!" he said, but he still wouldn't look at her. Pooja took it as proof.
Friday. Their cousin Rohit, visiting from Pune, said casually over dinner, "Pooja, sorry about your headphones. I stepped on them on Sunday. I thought I'd told you."
Pooja put down her spoon. She looked at Chetan, who was still staring at his plate. He always looked like that when he was scared of being blamed.
"Chetan," she said quietly. "I'm sorry."

qa.q: Who actually broke Pooja's headphones?
qa.a: Their cousin Rohit said he stepped on them on Sunday.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when Rohit admitted it?
qa.a: Pooja felt shocked and guilty, realising she had wrongly read Chetan's fidgeting as proof of lying.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Pooja do differently?
qa.a: She treated fidgeting and looking away as proof; next time she could ask calmly and look for facts before calling anyone a liar.

qa.q: What was it like for Chetan to be called a liar all week?
qa.a: Chetan felt hurt and scared, crying and staring at his plate because he was blamed for something he didn't do.

grounding: It shows a teenager believing fidgeting and averted eyes prove her brother lied, until the truth shows those cues were weak.

passage:
Vijay, you say you can always tell when your friends are lying? Let your Lavanya Nani, forty years a teacher, tell you about the first exam I ever invigilated.
There were two boys in the back row. One was shaking, wiping his hands on his trousers, looking everywhere except at me. The other sat calm as a lake. I was young and very sure of myself. I walked straight to the shaking boy and took his paper. "Where are the notes?"
There were no notes. He was just terrified of exams. His father had told him that if he failed he would be taken out of school.
The calm boy had the answers written on the inside of his shirt cuff. I found them only because he dropped his pen.
I apologised to the first boy in front of the whole class. And I never again trusted a trembling hand as proof of anything.

qa.q: Where did the calm boy have the answers written?
qa.a: On the inside of his shirt cuff.

qa.q: How did young Lavanya feel as she walked to the shaking boy?
qa.a: She felt confident and very sure of herself, believing his nervousness proved he was cheating.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Lavanya judged honesty?
qa.a: Finding the answers on the calm boy's cuff, after wrongly accusing the frightened one, showed her that nervous signs prove nothing.

qa.q: How might the shaking boy have felt when his paper was taken?
qa.a: He probably felt humiliated and even more frightened, already scared about failing and then wrongly accused.

grounding: A grandmother recalls wrongly reading a nervous student's trembling as proof of cheating, while the calm student was the one lying.

passage: With the school bus leaving in ten minutes and rain drumming on the tin roof, the class hunted for the missing lab register. Mehak watched Swati, who stood by the window twisting her dupatta and staring at the floor. "She's hiding something," Mehak whispered to her bench-mate. "Look, she won't even look at Ma'am." Meanwhile Rudra, who had been the last to use the register, answered every question with an easy smile. The teacher asked everyone to check their bags anyway. The register slid out of Rudra's folder. He shrugged. "Must have picked it up by mistake." Mehak felt her cheeks burn. On the bus she sat beside Swati, who admitted she always went stiff when a teacher asked questions, even when she had done nothing. Mehak stared at the wet window, thinking how sure she had felt, and how wrong.

qa.q: What was Swati doing while the class searched for the register?
qa.a: Swati stood by the window twisting her dupatta and staring at the floor.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when the register slid out of Rudra's folder?
qa.a: Mehak felt embarrassed and ashamed of her quick judgement; her cheeks burned because she had been so sure Swati's fidgeting meant guilt.

qa.q: What could Mehak do next time she is tempted to read guilt from someone's body language?
qa.a: She could remind herself that nervousness is not proof, wait for facts such as who last used the register, and keep her guess to herself instead of whispering it.

qa.q: What is it like for Swati when classmates read her stiffness as guilt?
qa.a: Swati goes stiff whenever a teacher asks questions, even when she has done nothing, so being suspected for it would feel unfair and make her even more tense.

grounding: Shows an observer who takes fidgeting and avoided eye contact as proof of lying, then sees that the nervous classmate was innocent while the calm one had the missing register.
